construction.entropy: 125 bits — 25 symbols of 5 bits, generated, never chosen by a human
construction.alphabet: Crockford Base32: 0123456789ABCDEFGHJKMNPQRSTVWXYZ (no I, L, O, U)
construction.generation: 25 bytes from crypto.getRandomValues(); symbol i = ALPHABET[byte_i & 0x1f]. 256 = 8 x 32, so the mask is uniform: no rejection sampling, no modulo bias
construction.display: Five groups of five, hyphen-separated, uppercase
construction.normalization: Drop hyphens and whitespace, uppercase, then O->0 and I->1 and L->1. U is rejected rather than folded. Exactly 25 symbols
construction.stretching: None. No Argon2id, no PBKDF2. At 125 generated bits an offline attack on the service-held envelope is infeasible without a work factor, and a work factor would make the argument conditional on hardware
construction.kdf: K_rec = HKDF-SHA256(ikm = utf8(canonical code), salt = salt[16], info = LP("done/recovery/v1") || LP(principal_id), L = 32)
construction.aad: LP("done/recovery/v1") || LP(principal_id) || LP(decimal v) || LP(hex r_pub)
construction.length_prefix: uint16be(byteLength) || utf8 — injective, so no field can shift another
construction.envelope: RecoveryEnvelope = { v: 1, salt: 16 bytes, nonce: 12 bytes, ct: AES-256-GCM over the 32-byte X25519 scalar, tag included }
construction.nonce_note: The salt is fresh per seal, so K_rec is fresh per seal and exactly one message is ever encrypted under it. Nonce reuse is structurally unreachable rather than avoided by discipline
construction.step_up: Replacement requires content access proven by use, plus a single-use service challenge SHA-256( LP("done/recovery-replace/v1") || LP(principal_id) || LP(hex SHA-256(new r_pub)) ) answered by the account credential. No freshness window: the challenge is bound to the operation
construction.not_carried: The code is never sent to the service, never persisted by the client, and never re-displayed once the account exists

keypair_kat.note: Alice's X25519 keypair. Used so the vector's own keypair is itself a known-answer test; the generator derives the public key from the scalar and fails if they do not match.

encoding_vectors.name: all-zero-bytes
encoding_vectors.why: Pins symbol 0. A code of all zeroes is a legal code, and an implementation that special-cases it is wrong.

encoding_vectors.name: ascending-bytes
encoding_vectors.why: Bytes 0x00..0x18 walk the first 25 symbols in order, pinning the alphabet itself.

encoding_vectors.name: high-bits-set
encoding_vectors.why: Bytes 0xE0..0xF8 must encode identically to 0x00..0x18. Proves the three discarded bits are discarded, and catches an implementation that reaches for a modulo instead of a mask.

encoding_vectors.name: generated-code
encoding_vectors.why: A realistic draw, and the code the seal vectors below use.

normalization_vectors.name: lowercase
normalization_vectors.why: A user transcribing into a phone keyboard gets lowercase for free.

normalization_vectors.name: letter-o-for-zero
normalization_vectors.why: The confusion Crockford exists to absorb, in the direction people actually make it.

normalization_vectors.name: letter-i-for-one
normalization_vectors.why: A handwritten 1 read back as I.

normalization_vectors.name: letter-l-for-one
normalization_vectors.why: The same 1 read back as l, which is the worse of the two in a sans-serif face.

normalization_vectors.name: spaces-instead-of-hyphens
normalization_vectors.why: Separators are presentation. Any run of them, anywhere, is dropped.

normalization_vectors.name: no-separators
normalization_vectors.why: Pasted out of a password manager that stored the canonical form.

normalization_vectors.name: mixed-confusables
normalization_vectors.why: Lowercase, both substitutions and the wrong separator at once — one person copying handwriting into a phone. Every rule fires on the same input, which is the case an implementation that applies them in the wrong order gets wrong.

rejected_inputs.reason: Contains U, which the generator can never emit
Punctuation is not a separator and not a symbol

seal_vectors.name: primary-envelope
seal_vectors.why: The envelope as account creation writes it, with RFC 7748 §6.1 as the recovery keypair.

seal_vectors.name: second-principal
seal_vectors.why: Same code, same salt, same nonce, different principal. Proves the principal is bound in both the derivation and the AAD — two principals on one profile is the ordinary path, not an attack (row 3 §3).

must_fail.name: wrong-code
must_fail.mutate: Change one symbol of the code, then derive and unseal.

must_fail.name: wrong-salt
must_fail.mutate: Derive with a salt of 16 zero bytes.

must_fail.name: wrong-principal
must_fail.mutate: Derive and authenticate against a second principal id. Changes both halves at once -- the AAD half alone is aad-only-other-principal.

must_fail.name: rebound-public-key
must_fail.mutate: Authenticate with Bob's public key in the AAD — the envelope re-paired with a public key that is not its own.

must_fail.name: downgraded-version
must_fail.mutate: Authenticate with v=0 in the AAD.

must_fail.name: flipped-tag-bit
must_fail.mutate: Flip the low bit of the final tag byte.

must_fail.name: truncated-ciphertext
must_fail.mutate: Drop the final byte of the sealed envelope.

must_fail.name: aad-only-other-principal
must_fail.mutate: The correct K_rec, with the AAD naming a second principal. Isolates the AAD binding from the derivation.

must_fail.name: aad-only-devicelock-label
must_fail.mutate: Authenticate with row 13's device-lock label. Both constructions seal a key under a 125-bit generated code, so the label is what stops a local device-lock seal being presented as this service-held envelope.

replacement_challenge_example.why: One worked challenge, so the binding is testable without a service.
